title: Car seat laws by state
methodology: Each state's child passenger safety law was read from the statute on the state's official legislature or code site. Where the official code host couldn't be read, we used the state's own highway safety, transportation or motor vehicle agency page, and say so in that state's sources. Multistate summaries (IIHS) were used only to find and cross-check the law; where they disagreed with the statute, the statute wins. A rule is recorded only when the law states it: rear-facing, harness, booster, seat belt and back-seat requirements, the first-offense fine and points, and exemptions. A state we couldn't confirm is marked unverified, and its page sends readers to the statute and the state agency. Best-practice guidance comes from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).

bestPractice.text: NHTSA: a child under age 1 should always ride rear-facing; keep children rear-facing as long as possible, until they reach the top height or weight limit of their car seat; then ride forward-facing with a harness and tether until that seat's top limit; then use a booster seat until the seat belt fits properly; keep children in the back seat at least through age 12. AAP: keep infants and toddlers rear-facing as long as possible, until the seat's highest rear-facing weight or height limit (most convertible seats allow rear-facing for 2 years or more); then a forward-facing harnessed seat as long as possible; then a belt-positioning booster until the adult belt fits, typically at about 4 feet 9 inches and 8 to 12 years old; all children younger than 13 should ride in the back seat.

rearFacing.text: keeping your child rear-facing as long as possible, until they reach the top height or weight limit allowed by the car seat's manufacturer. A child under age 1 should always ride rear-facing, and most convertible seats allow rear-facing for 2 years or more.

harness.text: using a forward-facing car seat with a harness and tether once your child outgrows the rear-facing limits, for as long as possible, up to the highest weight or height the seat's manufacturer allows.

booster.text: using a belt-positioning booster seat after your child outgrows the harnessed seat, until the vehicle seat belt fits properly, typically when they reach about 4 feet 9 inches tall and are 8 to 12 years old.

seatBelt.text: moving to the seat belt alone only when it fits: the lap belt lies snugly across the upper thighs, not the stomach, and the shoulder belt crosses the middle of the chest and shoulder, not the neck or face. Children big enough for the belt alone should always use a lap and shoulder belt.

backSeat.text: keeping all children younger than 13 in the back seat.

beltFitTest.text: The AAP says an adult seat belt fits when: the shoulder belt lies across the middle of the chest and shoulder, not the neck or throat; the lap belt is low and snug across the upper thighs, not the belly; and the child is tall enough to sit against the vehicle seat back with knees bent over the edge of the seat without slouching, and can stay that way for the whole trip. NHTSA uses the same lap-belt and shoulder-belt checks. The 5-step test, which California writes into law from January 1, 2027, asks: 1) Does the child sit all the way back against the seat? 2) Do the knees bend over the edge of the seat? 3) Does the shoulder belt snugly cross the center of the chest and shoulder, not the neck? 4) Is the lap belt as low as possible, touching the thighs? 5) Can the child stay seated like this for the whole trip?

inspections.text: Certified child passenger safety technicians check car seats at inspection stations nationwide. NHTSA says they inspect seats free of charge in most cases and show you how to install and use the seat correctly, and some locations offer virtual inspections. Search NHTSA's locator by ZIP code or city (it can filter for Spanish-speaking technicians), or find a technician through Safe Kids Worldwide.

federalStandard.text: Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 213 (49 CFR 571.213) sets requirements for child restraint systems used in motor vehicles and aircraft, with the stated purpose of reducing the number of children killed or injured in crashes. Manufacturers certify their own seats: NHTSA says the seats it rates are self-certified by the manufacturer to meet federal safety standards, including strict crash performance standards. Seats manufactured on or after December 5, 2026 must meet the updated FMVSS 213b. The new side-impact standard, FMVSS 213a (for seats used by children up to 40 pounds or 43 inches), has a compliance date of December 5, 2026, after a September 9, 2026 final rule moved it from June 30, 2025.

lawsVaryNote.text: State car seat laws set legal minimums, and many fall short of NHTSA and AAP guidance: Florida, Georgia and Indiana, for example, have no rear-facing requirement at all.

AL.summary: Alabama requires a rear-facing seat until at least age 1 or 20 pounds, a forward-facing seat until at least age 5 or 40 pounds, a booster until age 6, and a seat belt until age 15.

rearFacing.text: Infant-only seats and convertible seats used in the rear-facing position for infants until at least one year of age or 20 pounds.

harness.text: Convertible seats in the forward position or forward-facing seats until the child is at least five years of age or 40 pounds.

booster.text: Booster seats until the child is six years of age.

seatBelt.text: Seat belts until 15 years of age, so children 6 through 14 must be buckled in a seat belt.

backSeat.text: Alabama law doesn't say where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: Up to $25 per offense. The judge may dismiss the charge, with no court costs, on proof that you've acquired an appropriate child restraint. 1 point on a first offense, 2 points on a second or later offense.

AL.exemptions: Does not apply to taxis or to vehicles that seat 11 or more passengers. The law covers passenger cars, pickup trucks, vans seating 10 or fewer, minivans and SUVs.
AL.agencyName: Alabama Law Enforcement Agency; Alabama Department of Public Health
AL.notes: Statute text read from the Legislature's ALISON code database (history ends with Act 2014-300). Bills to extend the car seat ages died: HB18 (2025) was indefinitely postponed and HB32 (2026) stalled at second reading when the session adjourned April 9, 2026. 'At least one year of age or 20 pounds' and 'at least five years of age or 40 pounds' are the statute's exact words; the 'or' is ambiguous, so pages should quote it rather than interpret it.

AK.summary: Alaska requires a rear-facing seat for babies under 1 and for any child who weighs under 20 pounds, a car seat from age 1 to 4, and a booster from age 4 to 8 until the child reaches 57 inches or 65 pounds. Every child under 16 must be restrained.

rearFacing.text: A child less than one year old, or one year or older who weighs less than 20 pounds, must ride in a rear-facing child safety seat used according to the manufacturer's instructions.

harness.text: A child one year or older but under four who weighs 20 pounds or more must ride in a child restraint device used according to the manufacturer's instructions. The law doesn't specify a harness.

booster.text: A child over four but under eight who is under 57 inches tall and weighs at least 20 but less than 65 pounds must ride in a booster seat secured by a seat belt, or in another child restraint system.

seatBelt.text: A child over four who exceeds the booster height or weight limits (57 inches or 65 pounds) must wear a seat belt. Children 8 to 15 who are still under those limits ride in a child safety device or a seat belt, whichever the driver decides is appropriate.

backSeat.text: Alaska law doesn't say where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: The court bail schedule sets $50 for failing to provide a child safety device and $50 for failing to properly secure a child in one. A first charge for failing to provide a device may be dismissed on proof of correction; a second or later charge may not.

AK.exemptions: School buses (unless federally required to have belts), emergency vehicles, mail and newspaper delivery from inside the vehicle, vehicles not equipped with seat belts, people exempted by regulation, and motorcycles, off-highway vehicles and similar vehicles.
AK.agencyName: Alaska Highway Safety Office (Department of Transportation & Public Facilities)
AK.notes: Statute text from the Legislature's Alaska Statutes 2025. Fine from Administrative Rule 43.1 (the Court System's traffic bail schedule). Driver's-license points are not confirmed. The date of the last amendment is not confirmed. No 2026 amendment found. The Highway Safety Office page is old and has no law summary. GHSA's summary ('1 yr to under 5 yrs in an appropriate car seat or booster', '5 to under 8 yrs' booster) does not match the statute, which sets the car seat tier at 1 to under 4 and the booster tier at over 4 to under 8.

AZ.summary: Arizona requires children under 5 to ride in a child restraint system, and children 5 through 7 who are 4'9" or shorter to ride in a child restraint system such as a booster. There is no rear-facing requirement.

rearFacing.text: Arizona law has no rear-facing requirement.

harness.text: Children under five must be properly secured in a child restraint system. The law's definition of child restraint system includes booster seats, so it doesn't require a harnessed seat by age.

booster.text: Each passenger at least five but under eight years old who is not more than four feet nine inches tall must ride in a child restraint system (the definition includes booster seats).

seatBelt.text: Children 5 through 7 who are taller than 4'9" may use the seat belt. Arizona's separate seat belt law covers older children.

backSeat.text: Arizona law doesn't say where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: Civil penalty of $50, which is not imposed if you show the vehicle has since been equipped with a compliant child restraint system (for example, a receipt mailed to the court). The Governor's Office of Highway Safety notes that with court surcharges the total is often well over $100 in many jurisdictions, and that a Children Are Priceless Passengers class (a $35 fee that includes a seat if needed) can reduce the citation.

AZ.exemptions: Vehicles originally made without passenger restraints, recreational vehicles, commercial vehicles driven by a CDL holder, emergencies to get medical care, emergency vehicles taking a child for medical care, and cars too small to fit all the seats needed (if at least one child and as many others as reasonable are restrained).
AZ.agencyName: Arizona Governor's Office of Highway Safety
AZ.notes: The statute gives the $50 civil penalty; actual totals are higher with surcharges. The Arizona statute says 'not more than four feet nine inches tall', so a child who is exactly 57 inches still needs the restraint. The date of the last amendment is not confirmed.

AR.summary: Arkansas requires a child under 6 who weighs less than 60 pounds to ride in a child passenger safety seat. Once a child is 6 or weighs 60 pounds, a seat belt is enough, and every child under 15 must be restrained.

rearFacing.text: Arkansas law has no rear-facing requirement.

harness.text: The law requires a 'child passenger safety seat' (see the booster row) but doesn't specify a harnessed seat or a booster.

booster.text: A child who is less than six years of age and who weighs less than sixty pounds shall be restrained in a child passenger safety seat properly secured to the vehicle.

seatBelt.text: If a child is at least six years of age or at least 60 pounds, a safety belt properly secured to the vehicle meets the law. Drivers must restrain every child under 15.

backSeat.text: Arkansas law doesn't say where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: Fine of not less than $25 nor more than $100. If you show the court you have since acquired, purchased or rented an approved child passenger safety seat, the court may assess no more than the minimum fine. The court also considers whether the child was restrained by some other means, such as a seat belt.

AR.exemptions: Vehicles operated for hire. The law covers passenger cars, vans and pickup trucks.
AR.notes: The official code is on the LexisNexis public-access site, which hit a CAPTCHA on the full document. Its search results show the current text of 27-34-104(a) and the start of (b), plus 27-34-103(a)-(c). The full text of (b) and (c) comes from FindLaw (current as of March 28, 2024) and matches the Department of Public Safety's November 2024 driver manual, IIHS and GHSA. No 2025 amendment found. Arkansas has no dedicated state car seat web page; the agency link is the driver manual's law section.

CA.summary: California requires rear-facing until age 2 (unless the child is 40+ pounds or 40+ inches), a car seat or booster in the back seat until age 8 or 4'9", and a restraint or seat belt through age 15. From January 1, 2027, a child 8 to 15 may use the belt alone only if they pass the 5-step test.

rearFacing.text: A child under two must ride in a rear-facing child passenger restraint system unless the child weighs 40 or more pounds or is 40 or more inches tall, secured within the seat maker's height and weight limits.

harness.text: California law doesn't set an age for moving from a five-point harness to a booster (the CHP says the law does not address it).

booster.text: A child under eight must be properly secured in a rear seat in an appropriate child passenger restraint system. A child under eight who is 4'9" or taller may use a safety belt instead.

seatBelt.text: Children 8 through 15 must be secured in an appropriate child passenger restraint system or a safety belt. A child over 40 pounds may wear only a lap belt in the back seat if it has no lap-and-shoulder belt.

backSeat.text: Children under 8 must ride in the rear seat. Exceptions: no rear seat, side-facing jump seats, rear-facing rear seats, the restraint can't be installed properly in back, all rear seats are taken by children 7 or under, or a medical reason. A rear-facing seat may never go in front of an active frontal passenger airbag.

penalty.text: $100 for a first offense and $250 for a second or later one (before court penalty assessments). The court may reduce or waive the fine for an economically disadvantaged defendant who completes a community child passenger safety education program.

CA.exemptions: The court may exempt a child whose physical unfitness, medical condition or size makes a restraint impractical. Life-threatening emergencies and authorized emergency vehicles are exempt when no restraint is available (the child must use a seat belt). The section doesn't apply to a driver when the child's parent or legal guardian is a passenger.

pendingChange.text: AB 435 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 434) takes effect January 1, 2027. A child 8 to 15, or a child under 8 who is 4'9" or taller, will count as 'properly restrained by a safety belt' only if they pass all five steps of the 5-step test: sitting all the way back against the seat, knees bending over the seat edge, shoulder belt snug across the center of the chest and shoulder and not the neck, lap belt as low as possible and touching the thighs, and able to stay seated like this for the whole trip. Otherwise they must stay in a child passenger restraint system such as a booster.

CA.notes: The CHP page's fitStationUrl is the same page: it tells parents to contact a local CHP Area Office for a child passenger safety technician. Driver's-license points are not confirmed (IIHS reports California assesses points). Neither IIHS nor GHSA mentions the AB 435 change for 2027, and GHSA's California entry is garbled ('Children under 8 years old or have reached 4'9" ... may be secured by a booster seat').

CO.summary: Colorado requires rear-facing until age 2 (unless the child weighs 40+ pounds), a rear- or forward-facing car seat from 2 to 4, a car seat or booster until age 9, and the back seat (if there is one) until age 9. Children 9 through 17 need a belt or child restraint.

rearFacing.text: A child under two must ride in a rear seat if one is available, rear-facing if the child weighs under 40 pounds; at 40 pounds or more, rear- or forward-facing.

harness.text: A child two or older but under four who weighs at least 20 pounds must ride in a rear-facing or forward-facing child restraint system, in the rear seat if available.

booster.text: Every child under nine must be properly restrained in a child restraint system per the manufacturer's instructions. A child four or older but under nine who weighs at least 40 pounds must ride in a child restraint system or booster seat, in the rear seat if available.

seatBelt.text: Children 9 through 17 (until their 18th birthday) must use a safety belt or child restraint system. CDOT says a child can stop using a booster only at age 9 and only if the belt fits properly.

backSeat.text: Children under 9 must ride in the rear seat if one is available.

penalty.text: A class B traffic infraction: $65 penalty plus a $16 surcharge on the state schedule. The fine may be waived if you show the court, by your court appearance, that you've acquired, purchased or rented a child restraint system.

CO.exemptions: A child under 9 in a medical or other life-threatening emergency when no restraint is available; commercial vehicles operated by a child care center; for-hire common or contract carriers and luxury limousines. CDOT notes that buses, shuttle vans and taxis are exempt.
CO.notes: Text is the version effective January 1, 2025 from HB24-1055, as printed in the 2024 C.R.S. (the 2025 printout URL returned 404). The $65 plus $16 figure comes from the 2024 penalty schedule; IIHS's $81 matches. CDOT's inspection-station link points to NHTSA's locator, so fitStationUrl is null. CDOT's summary of the 2-3 tier says children under 20 pounds must ride rear-facing; the statute itself only covers 2-3 year olds who weigh at least 20 pounds.

CT.summary: Connecticut requires rear-facing with a 5-point harness until age 2 and 30 pounds, a 5-point harness until age 5 and 40 pounds, and a harness or booster until age 8 and 60 pounds. After that, a belt or child restraint through age 15.

rearFacing.text: A child under two years of age or weighing less than thirty pounds must ride rear-facing in a child restraint system equipped with a five-point harness.

harness.text: A child under five (but not under two), or weighing less than forty pounds (but not less than thirty), must ride rear- or forward-facing in a child restraint system with a five-point harness.

booster.text: A child under eight (but not under five), or weighing less than sixty pounds (but not less than forty), must ride in a five-point-harness seat or a booster seat secured by a seat safety belt. A booster may be used only with a belt that includes a shoulder belt.

seatBelt.text: A child eight or older and weighing 60 pounds or more may use an approved child restraint or a seat safety belt. Drivers must secure passengers 8 to 15 in a seat belt.

backSeat.text: No back seat rule, but a rear-facing seat may not go in the front seat of a vehicle with a functional passenger-side air bag.

penalty.text: A first violation is an infraction; a second is a fine of up to $199; a third or later is a class A misdemeanor. Anyone with a first or second violation must take a DMV child car seat safety course, and the DMV may suspend the license for up to two months for skipping it. The court may remit a first-time fine if you show proof within 14 days that you acquired, rented or bought an appropriate seat.

CT.exemptions: Children in student transportation vehicles follow separate rules (age 4 and up may use a belt). The child restraint rules don't apply on buses of one ton or more.
CT.notes: The first-offense dollar amount comes from the Superior Court infractions schedule, which I didn't reach on an official page, so fineFirst is null: IIHS says $50 and a local police page says $92. Last amended by P.A. 23-40 (fine remission); the age and weight tiers date from 2017. The 2026 OLR 'Acts Affecting Transportation' and 'Acts Affecting Children' reports list no car seat changes, and 14-100a isn't in the 2026 Supplement.

DE.summary: Delaware requires a rear-facing 5-point-harness seat for children under 2 and under 30 pounds, a 5-point harness for children under 4 and under 40 pounds, and a booster until the child outgrows it. Children under 12 who are 5'5" or shorter can't ride in front of an active air bag.

rearFacing.text: A child under the age of 2 years and less than 30 pounds must be properly secured in a rear-facing child restraint equipped with a 5-point harness.

harness.text: A child under the age of 4 and less than 40 pounds must be properly secured in a 5-point-harness restraint, rear- or forward-facing, until reaching the restraint's upper height or weight limits.

booster.text: A child must be properly secured in a belt-positioning booster until reaching the booster's upper height or weight limits per the manufacturer's guidelines.

seatBelt.text: A child who has reached the booster's upper height and weight limits and is under 16 must wear a properly secured seat belt in every seating position.

backSeat.text: A child under 12 who is 5'5" or shorter may not ride in the front passenger seat of a vehicle with an active passenger-side air bag, unless there's no rear seat or all rear seats are taken by other such children. This is a secondary offense.

penalty.text: A first offense brings no fine: police should refer the driver to an Office of Highway Safety car seat fitting station. A second or later violation is a $25 fine (plus court costs, per OHS).

DE.notes: SB 68 was approved June 30, 2023 and took effect one year later. Both tiers are 'under 2 AND under 30 pounds' and 'under 4 AND under 40 pounds' (Delaware OHS says the same). The booster stage has no age cap other than the under-16 scope of the law. The OHS page still contains an old quote ('up to 8 years of age or 65 lbs') from the pre-2024 law, so don't copy from it.

DC.summary: D.C. requires rear-facing until age 2 (unless the child is at least 40 pounds and 40 inches), a car seat until age 3, and an infant, convertible or booster seat until age 8. Children 8 to 15 need a seat belt or child restraint.

rearFacing.text: A child under 2 who weighs less than 40 pounds or measures less than 40 inches must be properly restrained in a rear-facing child restraint seat.

harness.text: A child under 3 must be properly restrained in a child restraint seat (one fastened to the vehicle by a seat belt, with all its securing straps in use).

booster.text: Children under 8 must be properly seated in an installed infant, convertible (toddler) or booster child safety seat, according to the manufacturer's instructions. A booster may only be used with both a lap and shoulder belt.

seatBelt.text: Every child under 16 must be restrained in an approved child safety restraint system or a seat belt, so children 8 to 15 may use the belt.

backSeat.text: No general back seat rule. A parent carrying more of their own children than there are belts may leave some unrestrained, but an unrestrained child may not ride in the front seat.

penalty.text: First offense: pay a $75 fine or attend a child restraint safety class ($25). Second: the class ($25) plus a $75 fine. Third: $125. Fourth and later: $150. Processed as a moving violation, with 2 points. The fine for a first violation of the under-3 rule is waived with proof you've since acquired an approved seat (purchase, gift or loan program).

DC.exemptions: The law applies to personal-use vehicles seating 8 or fewer passengers; it excludes livery, sightseeing, taxi, ambulance, funeral and farm vehicles.
DC.agencyName: District Department of Transportation (Child Safety Seat Program)
DC.notes: Statute wording for rear-facing: 'if the child weighs less than 40 pounds or measures less than 40 inches in length, and is under 2 years of age'. Read literally, a child under 2 can face forward only if they're at least 40 pounds AND 40 inches. IIHS and GHSA both summarize it as 'unless 40+ pounds OR 40+ inches'. GHSA also lists a 30-pound limit, a 57-inch cutoff and back seat rules for DC that aren't in the Code. DDOT gives District residents free car seats and boosters, and DC DMV does free inspections at 1001 Half Street SW.

FL.summary: Florida requires children through age 3 to ride in a separate carrier or integrated child seat, and children 4 and 5 to ride in a carrier, integrated seat or booster. From age 6, a seat belt is allowed. There is no rear-facing requirement.

rearFacing.text: Florida law has no rear-facing requirement.

harness.text: For children aged through 3 years, the restraint must be a separate carrier or a vehicle manufacturer's integrated child seat.

booster.text: For children aged 4 through 5 years, a separate carrier, an integrated child seat, or a child booster seat may be used.

seatBelt.text: Children 6 and older may use a seat belt, and all passengers under 18 must be belted or in a child restraint. A 4- or 5-year-old may use a seat belt instead only when carried free by a driver outside the immediate family, in a medical emergency, or with documented medical need.

backSeat.text: No Florida law says where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: A moving violation with a $60 base fine and 3 points on your license. With the court's approval, you can instead complete a child restraint safety program; then the points are waived and the fine and costs may be waived.

FL.exemptions: For-hire chauffeur-driven taxis, limousines, sedans, vans, buses and motor coaches; school buses; buses for hire; farm equipment; trucks over 26,000 lb GVWR; motorcycles, mopeds and bicycles. Ages 4-5 may use a belt in the three situations above.
FL.agencyName: Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles
FL.notes: The $60 is the s. 318.18(3)(a) base fine for moving violations; court costs are extra. Last amended by ch. 2020-69. 2026 HB 233 / SB 1384 (booster seats for ages 6 to 8) died in committee on 2026-03-13.

GA.summary: Georgia requires children under 8 to ride in a car seat or booster suited to their height and weight, in the back seat. A child under 8 who is over 4'9" may use a seat belt instead.

rearFacing.text: Georgia law has no rear-facing requirement.

harness.text: The law requires a child passenger restraining system appropriate for the child's height and weight (see the booster row), not a specific seat type.

booster.text: A child under 8 must be properly restrained in a child passenger restraining system appropriate for their height and weight, approved under FMVSS 213 and used per the manufacturer's directions. If the child's height is over 4'9", a seat belt is required instead.

seatBelt.text: Every minor 8 or older must wear a seat belt. A child under 8 who weighs at least 40 pounds may use a lap belt only when the vehicle has no lap-and-shoulder belts, or when they're all in use by other children.

backSeat.text: A child under 8 must ride in a rear seat, unless the vehicle has no rear seat suitable for a car seat or all of them are taken by other children.

penalty.text: First conviction: fine of not more than $50. Second or later: not more than $100. No court may add fees or surcharges. 1 point on a first offense, 2 points on a second or later offense.

GA.exemptions: Taxicabs and public transit vehicles; the rule covers passenger cars, vans and pickup trucks, and multifunction school activity buses need not carry children 5 or older in a car seat. A physician's written statement that a child's physical or medical condition prevents restraint.
GA.notes: The official O.C.G.A. is published through LexisNexis, which I didn't fetch. The statute text comes from GOHS's reproduction of § 40-8-76, cross-checked with the GOHS FAQ, IIHS and GHSA; statuteUrl is null for that reason. The point values come from the § 40-5-57 schedule as reproduced in a 2020 bill (existing-law text). The points are confirmed on the Department of Driver Services points schedule. Checked against the 2025 Code of Georgia: § 40-8-76 was last amended by Ga. L. 2011 (SB 88), and the GOHS reproduction predates that amendment, but the rules shown here match the current text. No 2025 or 2026 amendment found.

HI.summary: Hawaii requires rear-facing with a harness under age 2, a rear- or forward-facing harness seat from 2 to 4, and a harness seat or booster from 4 to 10. Children 7 to 9 who are over 4'9" may use a lap-and-shoulder belt.

rearFacing.text: A child under two must be properly restrained in a rear-facing child passenger restraint system with harness.

harness.text: A child two or older but under four must be properly restrained in a rear- or forward-facing child passenger restraint system with harness.

booster.text: A child four or older but under ten must be properly restrained in a harnessed child restraint or booster seat. A child seven or older but under ten who is over four feet nine inches may instead use a lap-and-shoulder belt.

seatBelt.text: Children 7 to 9 who are over 4'9" may use a correctly worn lap-and-shoulder belt. From age 10, the child restraint law no longer applies.

backSeat.text: Hawaii law doesn't say where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: First conviction: fine up to $100, a required child passenger restraint safety class (up to four hours), a $50 driver education assessment, a $10 neurotrauma surcharge, and up to a $10 trauma system surcharge. Second within three years: $250 to $500. Third or later within three years: $500 to $800.

HI.exemptions: Emergency, commercial (for-hire) and mass transit vehicles, plus any exemptions the Department of Transportation sets by rule.
HI.notes: Act 122 (2022) took effect June 27, 2022. HDOT's page says to call 808-527-2588 to book a car seat check and lists Seat Check Saturday sites. One HDOT sentence ('children need to ride in a booster seat until age 10 provided that the child is over 4'9" tall') is garbled; follow the statute. HDOT also notes a $25-per-year Hawaii tax credit for buying a booster or child safety seat.

ID.summary: Idaho requires children 6 and younger to ride in a child safety restraint that meets federal standard FMVSS 213. From age 7, the regular seat belt law applies. There is no rear-facing or back seat requirement.

rearFacing.text: Idaho law has no rear-facing requirement.

harness.text: The law requires a child safety restraint (see the booster row) but doesn't specify a harness or booster.

booster.text: A child six years of age or younger must be properly secured in a child safety restraint that meets federal motor vehicle safety standard no. 213 (car seats and boosters both meet it).

seatBelt.text: From age 7, every occupant must wear a safety restraint under Idaho's seat belt law.

backSeat.text: No general rule. If all seat belts are in use and a child goes unrestrained, that child must be placed in the rear seat if the vehicle has one.

penalty.text: The Idaho Supreme Court infraction schedule sets a $84 total: a $27.50 fixed penalty plus court costs and fees.

ID.exemptions: Applies only to noncommercial drivers in vehicles made with seat belts after January 1, 1966. Exempt when all seat belts are in use (the unrestrained child goes in back), and while a child is out of the seat for nursing or other immediate physiological needs.
ID.agencyName: Idaho Transportation Department, Office of Highway Safety
ID.notes: The $84 comes from the Supreme Court schedule amendment effective Nov. 27, 2023. A secondary search summary says the FY 2026 schedule also totals $84, but its PDF returned 404, so that isn't confirmed. The ITD page links to an interactive map of car seat inspection sites. The statute was last amended in 2005 and shows no 2026 change (the page says statutes update July 1 after each session).

IL.summary: Illinois requires rear-facing until age 2 (unless the child is 40+ pounds or 40+ inches) and an appropriate child restraint, which can be a booster, until age 8. Children 8 to 15 must wear a seat belt.

rearFacing.text: A child under 2 must be properly secured in a rear-facing child restraint system, unless the child weighs 40 or more pounds or is 40 or more inches tall.

harness.text: Illinois law doesn't require a harnessed seat by age. Children under 8 need an appropriate child restraint system, which includes boosters (see the booster row).

booster.text: A child under 8 must be properly secured in an appropriate child restraint system ('which also includes a booster seat'). The parent or guardian must give anyone transporting their child under 8 a child restraint system.

seatBelt.text: Children 8 through 15 must be secured in seat belts. A child over 40 pounds may ride in the back seat with only a lap belt if the back seat has no lap-and-shoulder belt.

backSeat.text: No Illinois law says where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: First violation: a petty offense with a $75 fine. Second or later: $200. On a first violation of the under-8 rule, you won't be convicted if you show the court you have an approved child restraint and completed an installation course with a certified technician.

IL.exemptions: A child whose physical disability prevents appropriate restraint, certified by a physician.
IL.notes: The rear-facing rule came in with P.A. 100-672, effective January 1, 2019. Driver's-license points are not confirmed (IIHS reports Illinois assesses points). The IDOT page says 'rear-facing car seat until the age of two' and leaves out the statute's 40-pound and 40-inch exception. IDOT's technician link points to NHTSA's locator.

IN.summary: Indiana requires children under 8 to ride in a child restraint system, which can be a booster, used per the manufacturer's instructions. Children 8 to 15 need a child restraint or seat belt. There is no rear-facing requirement.

rearFacing.text: Indiana law has no rear-facing requirement.

harness.text: Indiana law doesn't require a harnessed seat by age; the under-8 rule (see the booster row) covers any child restraint system.

booster.text: A child less than eight must be properly fastened and restrained by a child restraint system according to the manufacturer's instructions. The state says this can include a belt-positioning booster.

seatBelt.text: Children 8 through 15 must be properly fastened in a child restraint system or a safety belt. A child over 40 pounds may use a lap belt if the vehicle has no lap-and-shoulder belts, or if all of them outside the front seats are in use by other children.

backSeat.text: No Indiana law says where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: A Class D infraction, with a judgment of up to $25. If it's your first violation and you have or acquire a child restraint system, you're not liable for any costs or monetary judgment.

IN.exemptions: A child with a physical or medical condition that makes a restraint impractical, if the driver carries a certificate from a physician, physician assistant or advanced practice registered nurse and shows it to the officer or court.
IN.notes: Read from the 2026 Indiana Code. Section 2 was last amended by P.L.129-2018 (adding APRNs to the medical certificate). Judgments go to the state child restraint system account. ICJI funds about 103 free inspection stations.

IA.summary: Iowa requires a rear-facing seat for a child under 1 who weighs under 20 pounds, a child restraint system (a booster counts) until age 6, and a restraint or seat belt from 6 through 17.

rearFacing.text: A child under one year of age and weighing less than twenty pounds must be secured in a rear-facing child restraint system used according to the manufacturer's instructions.

harness.text: Iowa law doesn't require a harnessed seat by age. The under-6 rule (see the booster row) covers any child restraint system, including boosters.

booster.text: A child under six years of age must be secured by a child restraint system used according to the manufacturer's instructions. The definition includes belt-positioning and booster seats.

seatBelt.text: A child at least six but under eighteen must be secured by a child restraint system or by a safety belt or safety harness.

backSeat.text: No Iowa law says where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: A simple misdemeanor with a scheduled fine of $135. If it's your first charge under the age-6 rules and you had no child restraint, you won't be convicted if you show the court in time that you've since bought or acquired one.

IA.exemptions: Peace officers on duty; 1965 or older vehicles, emergency vehicles, buses, motor homes and motorsports recreational vehicles (except the front passenger seat); a child certified by a physician or physician assistant as having a condition that prevents restraint; and back seat riders when all belts are in use. In a taxi or rideshare, the parent or adult with the child gets the ticket.
IA.agencyName: Iowa Department of Public Safety, Governor's Traffic Safety Bureau
IA.notes: legis.iowa.gov would not resolve (DNS failure) for the whole session, so the Iowa Code 2026 PDFs for 321.446 and 805.8A were read from Internet Archive copies of the official files. HF 2344 (2026, from the Transportation Committee) would have moved rear-facing to age 2 and the restraint age to 8. It doesn't appear among the 204 bills in the Governor's 2026 signing releases, including the June 2 'final bills' release, so it was not enacted. The final bill history couldn't be pulled from the Legislature's site. Both rear-facing conditions apply together (under 1 AND under 20 pounds). GTSB's page has no law summary, and its technician link goes to a hospital (UnityPoint Blank Children's), so fitStationUrl is null.

KS.summary: Kansas requires children under 4 to ride in a child safety seat meeting FMVSS 213, and children 4 to 7 to keep using one (a booster qualifies) until they reach 80 pounds or 4'9". Children 8 to 13 must wear a seat belt.

rearFacing.text: Kansas law has no rear-facing requirement.

harness.text: A child under four must use an appropriate child passenger safety restraining system meeting FMVSS 213. The law doesn't say harness, and the same wording covers the 4-7 tier.

booster.text: A child four or older but under eight 'who weighs less than 80 pounds or is less than 4 feet 9 inches in height' must use an appropriate child passenger safety restraining system meeting FMVSS 213, such as a booster.

seatBelt.text: A child eight or older but under 14, 'or who weighs more than 80 pounds or is more than 4 feet 9 inches in height', must wear a safety belt. If a seat has only a lap belt, a child who would otherwise need a booster must use the lap belt.

backSeat.text: No Kansas law says where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: A $60 fine, waived for the under-8 rules if you show the court you've bought or acquired an appropriate seat (the officer must tell you this). Not counted as a moving violation. Multiple unrestrained children in one car count as one violation.

KS.exemptions: No violation if there are more children needing restraint than seating positions and all positions are in use by children. The law covers passenger cars and autocycles.
KS.agencyName: Kansas Department of Transportation (Kansas Traffic Safety Resource Office)
KS.notes: The 4-7 wording conflicts with itself: (a)(2) requires a restraint if the child is under 80 lb OR under 4'9", while (a)(3) allows a belt if the child is over 80 lb OR over 4'9". IIHS reads it as belt-eligible at either threshold. Pages should quote both clauses rather than resolve them. Last amended in 2015 (autocycles); the revisor's page was current as of 10/14/2026. KDOT's KTSRO page has no law summary.

KY.summary: Kentucky requires a car seat for children 40 inches tall or shorter, and a booster seat for children under 8 who are between 40 and 57 inches tall. The law has no rear-facing or back-seat requirement.

rearFacing.text: Kentucky law does not require rear-facing. The Office of Highway Safety's fact sheet advises rear-facing to at least age 1 and 20 pounds, with age 2 and 30 pounds as best practice.

harness.text: A child 40 inches tall or shorter must be properly secured in a child restraint system that meets federal motor vehicle safety standards. The law sets this by height, not age.

booster.text: A child under 8 who is between 40 and 57 inches tall must be properly secured in a child booster seat. A child of any age taller than 57 inches does not need a booster.

seatBelt.text: In a vehicle made after 1981, the driver and all passengers must wear a properly adjusted and fastened seat belt, unless the passenger is a child secured in a car seat or booster as the law requires.

backSeat.text: No Kentucky law says where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: Not using a required car seat carries a $50 fine. Not using a required booster carries a $30 fine. Neither fine adds court costs or fees. A first-time booster violator can have the charge dismissed, with no fees or costs, by showing proof they acquired a booster seat.

KY.exemptions: The section's definition of motor vehicle excludes motorcycles, motor-driven cycles, farm trucks registered for agricultural use only with a gross weight of one ton or more, and vehicles designed to carry more than 15 passengers.
KY.agencyName: Kentucky Transportation Cabinet, Office of Highway Safety
KY.notes: The KRS 189.125 text is effective July 15, 2016. The current booster thresholds (under 8, 40-57 inches) date from 2015 Ky. Acts ch. 91, effective June 24, 2015. KRS 189.990 was amended in 2026, effective July 15, 2026, and the fact sheet's car seat ($50) and booster ($30) fines are unchanged in that text. The OHS fact sheet says a child 'must' stay rear-facing to 1 year and 20 lb, but KRS 189.125 contains no rear-facing requirement, so this is agency guidance, not law. KYTC has no HTML car seat page, and the agency URL is its official fact sheet PDF. The fact sheet refers inspections to Safe Kids and cert.safekids.org, and no state-run inspection page exists. KRS 189.125 shows no amendment since 2016.

LA.summary: Louisiana requires rear-facing until at least age 2, a harnessed forward-facing seat until at least age 4, then a booster until at least age 9 or until the child outgrows it. Children under 13 must ride in the back seat when one is available.

rearFacing.text: A child younger than 2 must ride in a rear-facing child restraint until reaching the seat manufacturer's weight or height limit.

harness.text: A child at least 2 who has outgrown the rear-facing limits must ride in a forward-facing seat with an internal harness until reaching that seat's weight or height limit. The booster stage starts only at age 4 or older.

booster.text: A child at least 4 who has outgrown the forward-facing harness limits must ride in a belt-positioning booster with a lap-shoulder belt. A child moves to the adult belt at age 9, or sooner after outgrowing the booster's height or weight limits.

seatBelt.text: A child at least 9, or one who has outgrown the booster's limits, must use the adult seat belt fitted correctly: sitting all the way back, knees bent over the seat edge, lap belt across the thighs and lower hips, and shoulder belt across the center of the chest. The law covers all children under 18.

backSeat.text: A child younger than 13 must ride in the rear seat when one is available. If an active passenger air bag is present, a child younger than 6 or under 60 pounds must ride in the rear seat if one is available.

penalty.text: A first offense is a $100 fine. A second offense is $250 to $500, and a third or later offense is $500 plus court costs. If the only violation is using the wrong restraint for an otherwise restrained child, the fine is capped at $100, fees and court costs included. A violation is not a moving violation. Having no restraint at all is a primary offense. Using the wrong-size restraint is a secondary offense: a driver can be cited for it only when stopped for a moving violation.

LA.exemptions: The law does not apply to ambulances or other emergency vehicles, during an emergency that threatens a life, or to a child who for medical reasons cannot use a restraint. The definition of motor vehicle excludes school buses, church and private buses and RVs with more than 10 seats, commercial trucks, vans and taxis, trucks rated over 2,000 lb capacity, farm tractors and motorcycles.
LA.notes: The statute's last amendment is Acts 2019, No. 51. No 2025 or 2026 act amending 32:295 was found; 2026 SB 55 touches only the adult belt law, R.S. 32:295.1. The LHSC page says 'the fine for not being properly restrained is $50', which conflicts with R.S. 32:295(I) ($100 for a first child-restraint offense). The $50 figure appears to describe the adult seat belt law, so the statute governs here. The LHSC page lists fitting stations through a QR code and the facebook.com/buckleuplouisiana page.

ME.summary: Maine requires rear-facing under age 2 and a harnessed seat for children 2 and older who weigh less than 55 pounds. After that, a booster is required until the child is 8, 57 inches tall or 80 pounds. Children under 12 must ride in the rear seat if possible.

rearFacing.text: A child under 2 must ride in a rear-facing seat, or a convertible seat in the rear-facing position. A child in a convertible seat who exceeds its rear-facing weight or height limit may face forward.

harness.text: A child 2 or older who weighs less than 55 pounds must ride in a child restraint with an internal harness. If the child exceeds the harness seat's height limit first, they move to a federally approved belt-positioning seat.

booster.text: A child who weighs less than 80 pounds, is shorter than 57 inches and is under 8 must ride in a belt-positioning seat or other child restraint. A child who reaches any one of those limits may use a seat belt.

seatBelt.text: A child under 18 who is not required to use a car seat or booster must be properly secured in a seat belt. Passengers 18 and older and the driver must also be belted.

backSeat.text: The driver must ensure that a child under 12 is properly secured in the rear seat, if possible.

penalty.text: Each violation is a traffic infraction with a mandatory fine: $50 for a first offense, $125 for a second and $250 for a third or later offense. The court may not suspend the fine.

ME.exemptions: The car seat and booster rules don't apply to a child whose medical condition calls for a different restraint. That opinion must be in writing from a physician, nurse practitioner, physician associate, or child passenger safety technician with special needs training, must recommend the restraint and must explain why. The child must then ride in the recommended restraint.
ME.agencyName: Maine Department of Public Safety, Bureau of Highway Safety
ME.notes: The Revisor's page was extracted on 2026-10-05. The rear-facing and harness rules come from PL 2019, c. 299 and c. 577, and the harness subsection (2-B) was last amended by PL 2021, c. 293. Later changes (PL 2023, c. 634; PL 2025, c. 316 revisor's correction) affect only the adult medical exemption and wording. No pending change was found.

MD.summary: Maryland requires children under 2 to ride rear-facing, and children under 8 to ride in a car seat or booster unless they are 4 feet 9 inches or taller. Every child under 16 must use a car seat, booster or seat belt.

rearFacing.text: A child under 2 must ride in a rear-facing child safety seat until reaching the seat manufacturer's weight or height limit.

harness.text: Maryland law has no separate harness stage. Children under 8 must ride in a child safety seat, which can be a harnessed seat or a booster, following the seat and vehicle instructions.

booster.text: A child under 8 must ride in a child safety seat, booster seats included, unless the child is 4 feet 9 inches or taller.

seatBelt.text: A child under 16 must be secured in a child safety seat or a seat belt. A seat belt may not be used for more than one person at a time.

backSeat.text: No Maryland law says where in the car a child must sit. The health department notes that a rear-facing seat may not be placed in front of an active air bag.

penalty.text: A violation carries a $50 fine. A first violation of the rear-facing rule (a child under 2 in a seat that isn't rear-facing) gets a written warning. A judge may waive the fine if the driver had no car seat at the time, gets one before the hearing and shows proof to the court. A violation is not a moving violation, so it adds no points. Failing to restrain several children in the same trip counts as a single violation.

MD.exemptions: Not a violation if a physician licensed in the state where the vehicle is registered certifies in writing that a car seat is impractical for the child because of weight, height, physical unfitness or another medical reason. The law covers Class A (passenger), Class E (truck) and Class M (multipurpose) vehicles. The health department says taxis are exempt and ride-share vehicles are not.
MD.agencyName: Maryland Department of Health, Kids In Safety Seats (KISS)
MD.notes: The rear-facing requirement and the first-offense written warning came from Chapter 232 of 2022 (SB 176), which took effect Oct. 1, 2022. The statute requires a 'child safety seat', which the law defines to include boosters, rather than a booster specifically. No pending change was found. The KISS page links to car seat events but no state inspection-station page, so fitStationUrl is null.

MA.summary: Massachusetts requires children under 8 to ride in a car seat or booster unless they are more than 57 inches tall. Children under 13 who have outgrown that requirement must wear a seat belt.

rearFacing.text: Massachusetts law does not require rear-facing.

harness.text: Massachusetts law has no separate harness stage. Children under 8 must ride in a federally approved child passenger restraint, either a car seat or a booster.

booster.text: A passenger under 8 must be secured in a child passenger restraint, fastened according to the manufacturer's instructions, unless the child is more than 57 inches tall.

seatBelt.text: A passenger under 13 who is not required to use a child passenger restraint must wear a properly adjusted and fastened safety belt.

backSeat.text: No Massachusetts law says where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: A driver who violates the law faces a fine of up to $25. The fine does not apply to a taxi driver whose cab has no child restraint. A violation is not counted as a moving violation for car-insurance surcharge purposes, and a citation can be contested.

MA.exemptions: The law does not apply to a child riding a school bus, a child in a vehicle made before July 1, 1966 that has no seat belts, or a child a physician certifies in writing as physically unable to use a conventional or special-needs restraint.
MA.notes: The current text of the first two paragraphs comes from Acts of 2008, ch. 79, approved April 11, 2008. Town police pages put its effective date at July 10, 2008, but no state source confirmed that date. The statute's exception is 'more than 57 inches'; IIHS describes it as 'at least 57 inches', a small wording difference. Mass.gov returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so the agency page is linked but was not read and isn't used as a fact source. The office that publishes it is also unconfirmed. Rear-facing bills (S.1703, H.2603, S.1657) are pending in the 2025-2026 session, but none was found to have been enacted, so pendingChange is null.

MI.summary: Since April 2, 2025, Michigan requires rear-facing until age 2, a harnessed forward-facing seat until age 5, and a booster until age 8 or 4 feet 9 inches. Each stage can end sooner if the child reaches the seat's limits. Children under 13 must ride in the rear seat if the vehicle has one.

rearFacing.text: A child must ride rear-facing until reaching the seat manufacturer's rear-facing weight or height limit or turning 2, whichever comes first.

harness.text: A child must then ride in a forward-facing seat with an internal harness until reaching that seat's weight or height limit or turning 5, whichever comes first.

booster.text: A child must then ride in a belt-positioning booster with a lap-shoulder belt until reaching 4 feet 9 inches or turning 8.

seatBelt.text: A child who is 8 or older, or 4 feet 9 inches or taller, and under 13 must wear a properly adjusted and fastened safety belt, and may keep using a booster within its limits. Children 13 to 15 must be belted under § 257.710e, which also requires the driver and front-seat passengers to wear belts.

backSeat.text: Children under 13 must ride in a rear seat if the vehicle has one. A child may sit in front only if all available rear seats are occupied by children. A rear-facing seat may go in front only if the passenger air bag is turned off.

penalty.text: A violation is a civil infraction with a fine of up to $10 plus court costs. No points are assessed, and no abstract goes to the Secretary of State. The court may waive the fine, costs and assessments if, before the appearance date, the driver shows proof of getting a compliant car seat and of receiving education from a certified child passenger safety technician.

MI.exemptions: The law does not apply in a bus, school bus, taxicab, moped, motorcycle or any vehicle not required to have seat belts under federal law. The Secretary of State may exempt, by rule, children for whom a car seat is impractical because of physical unfitness, a medical problem or body size.
MI.agencyName: Michigan State Police, Office of Highway Safety Planning
MI.notes: 2024 PA 21, effective April 2, 2025, rewrote § 257.710d with the staged rear-facing, harness, booster and rear-seat rules. The fine waiver (§ 257.907(11)) now requires both proof of seat acquisition and CPST education, as of the effective date of 2024 PA 22. The MCL site is complete through PA 103 of 2026, and § 257.710d shows no later amendment. Michigan's stage thresholds end at the age or the seat limit, whichever comes first, so a child may legally leave a stage before the listed age. The OHSP page links a car seat technician finder and the NHTSA fitting station locator.

MN.summary: Children ride rear-facing until at least age 2, in a harnessed seat until at least 4, and in a booster until 9 or until they outgrow it; each move up happens only after the child outgrows the current seat's height or weight limit. Children under 13 must ride in the back seat when one is available.

rearFacing.text: A child under 2 must be properly restrained in a rear-facing child restraint with an internal harness until the child reaches that seat's height or weight limit.

harness.text: A child at least 2 who has outgrown the rear-facing seat must ride forward-facing with an internal harness until reaching that seat's height or weight limit. A booster is allowed only from age 4, after the child outgrows the forward-facing seat.

booster.text: A child at least 4 who has outgrown the forward-facing harness must ride in a booster seat with a seat belt until age 9 or until the child outgrows the booster.

seatBelt.text: A child who is at least 9, or has outgrown the booster, may use the seat belt alone if it fits: back against the seat, knees bent over the edge, lap belt low on the thighs and hips, shoulder belt across the chest and not the neck. All passengers under 18 must be restrained. When a child fits more than one stage, the more protective stage applies.

backSeat.text: Children under 13 must ride in the rear seat when one is available. A child under 6 or under 60 pounds must ride in the rear seat if the vehicle has an active passenger-side airbag and a rear seat is available.

penalty.text: A violation is a petty misdemeanor with a fine of up to $50. The fine may be waived or reduced if the driver shows that, within 14 days, they bought or obtained a federally approved child restraint for their own use.

MN.exemptions: Emergency medical vehicles; peace officers on duty (who must use a seat belt instead); drivers for hire such as taxis and buses; school buses over 10,000 pounds GVWR; and a child who, in a licensed physician's judgment, cannot safely ride in a restraint (the driver must carry a typewritten physician statement dated within the previous six months). Rental companies must provide a child restraint on request and may charge a reasonable fee.
MN.agencyName: Minnesota Department of Public Safety, Office of Traffic Safety
MN.notes: Current stage rules come from 2024 Minn. Laws ch. 104, art. 1, §§ 40-44, effective Aug. 1, 2024 per DPS. The DPS page sends readers to buckleupmn.org for car seat checks, but that site belongs to the Minnesota Safety Council, a nonprofit, not a state agency, so fitStationUrl is null. IIHS agrees with the statute.

MS.summary: Children under 4 must ride in a child safety seat. Children 4 to 6 must use a belt-positioning booster if they are shorter than 4'9" or weigh less than 65 pounds.

rearFacing.text: Mississippi law has no rear-facing requirement. The state health department recommends rear-facing seats.

harness.text: A child under 4 must be protected by a child passenger restraint device or system that meets federal safety standards. The law doesn't say which type.

booster.text: A child who is at least 4 but under 7 must use a belt-positioning booster seat if the child is shorter than 4 feet 9 inches or weighs less than 65 pounds. If more than two children need boosters and the rear seat has only two lap-and-shoulder belts, only the two children in those seats need boosters; the others may use a lap belt.

seatBelt.text: At 7, or between 4 and 6 once the child is at least 4'9" and at least 65 pounds, the child moves to the seat belt. Mississippi's seat belt law (§ 63-2-1) requires every passenger in a passenger vehicle, in every seat, to wear a fastened belt.

backSeat.text: No Mississippi law says where in the car a child must sit. The state health department advises children under 13 to ride in the back seat.

penalty.text: A violation of § 63-7-301 is punishable by a fine of not more than $25 for each offense (§ 63-7-309).

MS.exemptions: The law covers passenger motor vehicles built to carry 15 or fewer people. It doesn't apply to vehicles excluded from the seat belt law: farm-use vehicles, implements of husbandry and farm tractors; passenger cars driven by rural mail carriers or utility meter readers on duty; and buses (§§ 63-7-301(2), 63-2-1(3)).
MS.notes: The Mississippi Legislature's official free code is hosted by LexisNexis (linked from legislature.ms.gov) and has no stable per-section URLs. Current §§ 63-7-301 and 63-7-309 text was read from 2026 HB 1022, which reprinted § 63-7-301 unchanged and would have raised the § 63-7-309 fine from $25 to $100. That bill died in committee on 02/03/2026, so the $25 maximum still applies. 2024 HB 1008, which would have made this a primary offense, also died. Discrepancy: the statute requires a booster for ages 4 to 6 if the child is 'less than 4 feet 9 inches in height or weighs less than sixty-five pounds,' so a child must meet both measures to skip it. The MSDH page and IIHS instead say a child may use an adult belt at 57 inches OR 65 pounds. The fields above follow the statute. The MSDH page (last reviewed Oct. 4, 2024) offers car seat inspection help at 601-206-1010. The year of the last amendment wasn't confirmed from an official source, so effective is null.

MO.summary: Children under 4, or under 40 pounds, must ride in a child safety seat. Children 4 to 7 who weigh 40 to 79 pounds and are under 4'9" must use a car seat or booster; once a child weighs 80 pounds or is taller than 4'9", a seat belt or booster is allowed.

rearFacing.text: Missouri law has no rear-facing requirement.

harness.text: Children under 4, regardless of weight, and children under 40 pounds, regardless of age, must be secured in a child passenger restraint system. MoDOT describes this as a rear-facing or forward-facing harness seat.

booster.text: Children at least 4 but under 8 who weigh at least 40 but under 80 pounds and are shorter than 4'9" must be secured in a child passenger restraint system or booster seat. A child who would need a booster may ride with a lap belt only in a back seat that has no lap-and-shoulder belt for the booster.

seatBelt.text: Children who weigh at least 80 pounds or are taller than 4'9" must be secured by a seat belt or a booster appropriate for the child. Drivers are responsible for restraining every passenger under 16 (§§ 307.178, 307.179).

backSeat.text: No Missouri law requires children to ride in the back seat. When there are more children than seating positions, children who can't be restrained must ride behind the front seat if the vehicle has a back seat.

penalty.text: Violating the car seat or booster rules is an infraction with a fine of up to $50 plus court costs. The charge is dismissed or withdrawn if the driver shows, before or at the hearing, that they acquired the required seat. For a child who is 80 pounds or more or taller than 4'9", the penalty is the seat belt law's: a fine of up to $10, with no court costs and no points (§ 307.178.6).

MO.exemptions: Public carriers for hire, and students 4 and older riding a school bus designed for 11 or more passengers that meets Missouri school bus standards.
MO.agencyName: Missouri Department of Transportation (Missouri Coalition for Roadway Safety)
MO.notes: Bills adding a rear-facing rule were introduced in 2025 (SB 497) and 2026 (SB 1007, HB 2170). As of 2026-10-14, the Revisor shows § 307.179 unchanged since its 28 Aug 2006 version, with no newer or future version, so none of those bills took effect. The statute doesn't address children 8 to 15 who weigh under 80 pounds and are 4'9" or shorter; MoDOT says children 8 and up use a booster or seat belt. IIHS agrees with the statute.

MT.summary: Children under 2 must ride rear-facing; from 2 to 4, in a rear- or forward-facing seat with a harness; and from 4 to 8, in a forward-facing harnessed seat or a booster. A child moves to the adult seat belt at 9, or earlier after outgrowing the booster's height or weight limit.

rearFacing.text: A child under 2 years of age must ride in a rear-facing child safety restraint that meets federal motor vehicle safety standards.

harness.text: A child between 2 and up to 4 years of age must ride in a rear-facing or forward-facing child safety restraint with an internal harness.

booster.text: A child between 4 and up to 8 years of age must ride in a forward-facing harnessed restraint or a booster seat used with a lap-and-shoulder belt. The adult belt is required at 9, or once the child outgrows the booster's manufacturer height or weight limits, whichever comes first.

seatBelt.text: A passenger who is at least 9, or who has outgrown the booster's manufacturer height or weight limits (whichever comes first), must be secured with an adult seat belt. Every child restraint must be installed and used according to the manufacturer's instructions.

backSeat.text: No Montana law says where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: A violation is punishable by a fine of up to $100. The fine must be waived if, within 7 days of the violation, the driver gives the charging officer's office proof of acquiring an appropriate child restraint. The waiver isn't available if a previous violation was already dismissed this way.

MT.exemptions: Motor homes, school buses, taxicabs, farm tractors, bicycles, mopeds, quadricycles, motorcycles and motor-driven cycles; vehicles not federally required to have seat belts; ambulances and other authorized emergency vehicles; and an emergency that threatens the life of the driver or the child. The Department of Transportation may by rule exempt a child whose physical or medical condition or body size prevents use of a restraint.
MT.notes: This replaces Montana's old rule (a restraint for children under 6 and under 60 pounds). HB 586 (Ch. 692, L. 2025) took effect October 1, 2025, per MDT; MCA 2025 shows the new text. The statute says 'between 4 years of age and up to 8 years of age' for the harness-or-booster stage and makes the adult belt mandatory 'at least 9 years of age,' so it doesn't clearly place 8-year-olds. MDT reads it as booster from ages 4 to 8 and adult belt from 9 (after the booster is outgrown), and booster.untilAge = 9 follows that. IIHS lists the booster stage as 4 to under 8 and the adult belt as permissible from ages 8 to 9, a slightly earlier reading. MDT's page says waiver proof goes to the 'court of jurisdiction,' but the statute says the 'office of the charging officer,' and the fields follow the statute.

NE.summary: Children under 2 must ride rear-facing until they outgrow the seat's height or weight limit. All children under 8 must ride in a federally approved child safety seat in a back seat when one is available, and children 8 to 17 must wear a seat belt.

rearFacing.text: All children up to 2 years of age must use a rear-facing child restraint until they outgrow the manufacturer's maximum height or weight for that seat.

harness.text: Nebraska law sets no separate harness age. Children under 8 must use a federally approved child restraint, which can be a harnessed seat or a booster.

booster.text: All children up to 8 years of age must ride in a child passenger restraint system that meets Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 213 (a car seat or booster), correctly installed per the manufacturer's instructions.

seatBelt.text: Children from 8 up to 18 must be secured by an occupant protection system (seat belt); NDOT says a booster also satisfies the law. This 8-to-18 rule is enforced only as a secondary action, after the driver is cited for something else.

backSeat.text: Children under 8 must ride in a seat other than the front seat if that seat has a restraint system and isn't already taken by other children under 8.

penalty.text: A violation is an infraction with a $25 fine per violation, and failing to restrain several children at once counts as one offense (§ 60-6,268). NDOT says court costs are added and 1 point is assessed against the driver's record. The under-8 rules are primary enforcement.

NE.exemptions: Taxicabs, mopeds, motorcycles, and vehicles of model year 1963 or earlier without occupant protection; a child whose physician certifies a restraint would be harmful because of weight, physical condition or another medical reason (the driver must carry a signed statement); drivers of authorized emergency vehicles on duty; and vehicles in a lawful parade or exhibition.
NE.agencyName: Nebraska Department of Transportation, Highway Safety Office
NE.notes: The current rules come from LB 42 (2018), effective January 1, 2019, per NDOT. On points: § 60-6,268 doesn't mention them. The § 60-4,182 one-point catch-all excludes only occupant-protection violations under § 60-6,270 (the adult belt law), which fits NDOT's statement of 1 point. NDOT's CPS page links to a PDF list of inspection stations at dot.nebraska.gov/media/jhvftuqy/ne-inspection-stations.pdf. IIHS agrees with the statute.

NV.summary: Children under 6 who are shorter than 57 inches must ride in a child restraint (car seat or booster), and children under 2 must ride rear-facing in the back seat. Passengers 6 and older, or 57 inches or taller, must wear a seat belt.

rearFacing.text: A child under 2 must be secured in a rear-facing child restraint in the back seat. The child may ride rear-facing in the front passenger seat, with the airbag deactivated, only if a physician's signed statement says the child's special health care needs require it, if all back seats are taken by other children under 2, or if the vehicle has no back seat.

harness.text: Nevada law sets no separate harness stage. A child under 6 and under 57 inches must use a child restraint appropriate for the child's size and weight.

booster.text: A child under 6 years of age and less than 57 inches tall must be secured in a federally approved child restraint system appropriate for the child's size and weight, installed per the manufacturer's instructions. The law's definition includes booster seats.

seatBelt.text: Passengers 6 or older, or 57 inches or taller regardless of age, must wear a seat belt in the front or back seat (NRS 484D.495). The driver is cited for an unbelted child under 18. Belt violations are enforced only after a stop for another violation, with a civil penalty of up to $25.

backSeat.text: Children under 2 must ride rear-facing in the back seat, with the front-seat exceptions listed under rear-facing. There is no back-seat rule for older children.

penalty.text: A violation is a misdemeanor. First offense: $100–$500 fine or 10–50 hours of community service. Second: $500–$1,000 or 50–100 hours. Third or later: license suspension for 30 to 180 days. Completing a DPS-approved training program within 60 days of sentencing waives a first-offense fine or community service and halves a second-offense one. It is not a moving traffic violation, so no demerit points.

NV.exemptions: Public transportation, including taxicabs, school buses and emergency vehicles; and a child whom a physician or advanced practice registered nurse finds a restraint would be impractical or dangerous for because of weight or physical or medical condition (a signed statement must be carried in the vehicle).
NV.agencyName: Nevada Department of Public Safety, Office of Traffic Safety
NV.notes: The NRS chapter page is revised through 9/9/2026, which includes the 2025 session. The section's last amendments are 2021 (Stats. 2021 pp. 176 and 3328), with no 2023 or 2025 change. News reports say the rear-facing rule (AB 118, 2021) began January 1, 2022, but no official page confirmed that date, so effective gives only the year. The OTS Occupant Protection page doesn't restate the law. It links to Safe Kids and a Nevada CPS resources PDF and has no state inspection-station page, so fitStationUrl is null. IIHS agrees, except that it lists the back-seat rule as '2 and under' where the statute says under 2.

NH.summary: New Hampshire requires children under 2 to ride rear-facing and children under 7 to ride in a car seat or booster unless they are at least 57 inches tall. Everyone under 18 must be buckled up.

rearFacing.text: A passenger under 2 must be secured in a rear-facing child restraint system that meets federal safety standards. The statute has no exception for a child who outgrows a rear-facing seat.

harness.text: New Hampshire law has no separate harness stage. Children under 7 must ride in a federally approved child restraint, used within the maker's height and weight limits.

booster.text: A passenger under 7 must be secured in a federally approved child restraint system, used according to the maker's instructions, including its height and weight limits. The rule doesn't apply once the child is 57 inches or taller.

seatBelt.text: Passengers under 18 who are not in a child restraint must wear a properly adjusted and fastened seat belt. Drivers under 18 must also buckle up.

backSeat.text: No New Hampshire law says where in the car a child must sit.

penalty.text: A violation carries a $50 fine for a first offense and $100 for a second or later offense. It is a violation, not a crime.

NH.exemptions: The law doesn't apply to vehicles regularly used to carry passengers for hire, school buses over 10,000 pounds (or lighter school buses built without belts), a child whose individualized education program says restraints are contraindicated, vehicles made before 1968, motorcycles, antique vehicles, farm tractors, or parade vehicles going no more than 10 mph.
NH.agencyName: New Hampshire Department of Safety, Office of Highway Safety
NH.notes: The rear-facing rule (paragraph I-c) was added by 2023, 163:1, effective 2024-01-01, per the statute's history line. Every core rule, including the fine, is in the statute itself. The Office of Highway Safety site returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so it is linked but not read and isn't used as a fact source. The statute doesn't mention license points. IIHS (October 2026) matches the statute.

NJ.summary: New Jersey requires children under 8 and under 57 inches to ride in a car seat or booster in the back seat: rear-facing under 2 and 30 pounds, a five-point harness under 4 and 40 pounds, then a booster. Older children must wear a seat belt.

rearFacing.text: A child under 2 and under 30 pounds must ride in a rear-facing seat with a five-point harness.

harness.text: A child under 4 and under 40 pounds must ride in a rear-facing seat with a five-point harness until outgrowing its top height or weight limit, then in a forward-facing seat with a five-point harness.

booster.text: A child under 8 and under 57 inches must ride in a forward-facing seat with a five-point harness until outgrowing its top height or weight limit, then in a belt-positioning booster seat.

seatBelt.text: A child who is 8 or older, or under 8 but at least 57 inches tall, must wear a properly adjusted and fastened seat belt. The driver must make sure every passenger under 18 is belted.

backSeat.text: Children under 8 and under 57 inches must ride in a rear seat. If the vehicle has no rear seat, the child may ride in front in a car seat or booster, but never in a rear-facing seat in front of a passenger airbag that is on.

penalty.text: A violation carries a fine of $50 to $75.

NJ.exemptions: The law covers motor vehicles equipped with seat belts or LATCH. It doesn't apply to school buses.
NJ.agencyName: New Jersey Division of Highway Traffic Safety
NJ.notes: The current text comes from P.L.2015, c.50, approved 2015-05-07. Its effective-date clause is 'the first day of the fourth month next following enactment', which works out to 2015-09-01. The Legislature's consolidated statutes have no stable per-section link, so statuteUrl points to the enacted chapter law on the Legislature's site. The fine is in N.J.S.A. 39:3-76.2d as amended by the same act. The statute doesn't mention license points. The Division of Highway Traffic Safety page cites P.L.2015, c.50 and matches it, and it lists county car seat inspection sites. IIHS (October 2026) matches the statute.

NM.summary: New Mexico requires a rear-facing seat in the back seat under age 1, a child safety seat through age 4 (or under 40 pounds), and a booster or car seat for ages 5 and 6 (or under 60 pounds). Children 7 through 12 may use a car seat or a seat belt, and everyone under 18 must be restrained.

rearFacing.text: Children under 1 must ride in a rear-facing child restraint that meets federal standards, in the rear seat if the vehicle has one.

harness.text: Children 1 through 4, regardless of weight, and children under 40 pounds, regardless of age, must ride in a child passenger restraint device that meets federal standards. The statute doesn't say it must have a harness.

booster.text: Children 5 and 6, regardless of weight, and children under 60 pounds, regardless of age, must ride in a booster seat or a child restraint that meets federal standards.

seatBelt.text: Children 7 through 12 may use a child restraint or a seat belt. A child is properly belted when the lap belt lies across the thighs and hips, not the stomach, and the shoulder belt crosses the chest, not the neck. Every passenger under 18 must be in a child restraint or a seat belt.

backSeat.text: A child under 1 must ride rear-facing in the rear seat if the vehicle has one. If there's no rear seat, the child may ride in front if the passenger airbag is deactivated or the vehicle has no deactivation switch.

penalty.text: The penalty assessment for a child not in a restraint device or seat belt is $25. The violation adds 2 points to the driver's license.

NM.exemptions: Authorized emergency vehicles, public transportation and school buses are exempt. The rules also don't apply when every seating position with a seat belt is occupied.
NM.notes: The current text comes from Laws 2005, ch. 298 (SB 586, signed 2005-04-07). The 2026 bill SB 313 reprints § 66-7-369 with subsections A through C unchanged, which confirms the text is still current; that bill died. New Mexico's codified statutes have no stable per-section link on the Legislature's site, so statuteUrl points to the enacted 2005 bill. The $25 fine is the existing-law amount in the § 66-8-116 penalty assessment schedule, as reprinted in 2025 SB 265 (which would have raised it to $100 and died). The 2 points come from 18.19.5.52(G) NMAC. The MVD page differs from the statute in two places: it says rear-facing 'until at least age 1 and 20 pounds' (the statute says under 1, with no weight) and that children 7 to 12 'must' use a booster (the statute allows a child restraint or a seat belt from 7). The statute governs. NMDOT runs fitting stations, but its traffic safety page has no station list, so fitStationUrl is null. IIHS (October 2026) matches the statute.

NY.summary: New York requires children under 2 to ride rear-facing (unless they outgrow the seat), children under 4 to ride in a child safety seat, and children under 8 to ride in an appropriate child restraint such as a booster. Passengers 8 through 15 must wear a seat belt.

rearFacing.text: A child under 2 must ride in a rear-facing child safety seat. If the child is taller or heavier than the seat maker's rear-facing limits, the seat may face forward.

harness.text: Children under 4 must ride in a federally approved child safety seat. A child under 4 who weighs more than 40 pounds may instead use an appropriate child restraint system with the lap and shoulder belt, or a lap belt if no lap and shoulder belt is available.

booster.text: Children 4 through 7 must ride in an appropriate child restraint system (a car seat or booster) used with the lap and shoulder belt, or a lap belt if no lap and shoulder belt is available. It is a defense to a ticket if the child is belted and is taller than 4'9" or heavier than 100 pounds.

seatBelt.text: Passengers 8 through 15 must wear a seat belt in any seat, and the driver is responsible for them. Passengers 16 and older must also buckle up.

backSeat.text: No New York law says where in the car a child must sit. The Governor's Traffic Safety Committee recommends the back seat for all children under 13.

penalty.text: A violation carries a civil fine of $25 to $100, plus 3 driver license points for a restraint violation involving a passenger under 16. For a child under 8, the court waives the fine if the driver shows they bought or rented a proper child restraint before the court date. The waiver doesn't apply to a second or later conviction.

NY.exemptions: School buses and authorized emergency vehicles are outside the law, except fire vehicles and volunteer ambulances. A passenger or driver with a physical disability that prevents restraint use, certified by a physician or nurse practitioner, is exempt. Taxis, liveries and charter buses have separate, narrower rules.
NY.agencyName: New York State Governor's Traffic Safety Committee
NY.notes: The rear-facing rule took effect 2019-11-01, per the Governor's Traffic Safety Committee. The 3 points come from the DMV point schedule ('Safety restraint violation involving person under 16'). GTSC describes the under-4 stage as a forward-facing harness seat, but the statute lets a child under 4 who weighs more than 40 pounds use a belt-positioning child restraint; the statute governs.
